concepts.text: SMP, NUMA, multiport memory and speed-up in numbers:
items: SMP (Stallings): two or more similar processors of comparable capability share main memory and I/O over a bus or other interconnect with about the same access time, all can perform the same functions, and one integrated operating system controls them. A master–slave arrangement in which only one processor runs the OS is not symmetric.

NUMA average access time = p_local × t_local + (1 − p_local) × t_remote; with 90% local references at 80 ns and 10% remote at 500 ns it is 72 + 50 = 122 ns, so the OS tries to place a process's pages in its own node's memory. CC-NUMA adds hardware cache coherence, usually with a directory.

Multiport memory with P processors and M modules needs P ports on every module and P × M processor–module paths, with fixed port priorities resolving conflicts; this is why it suits only small systems.

Amdahl's law rearranged gives the parallel fraction needed for a target speed-up S on N processors: f = (1 − 1/S) / (1 − 1/N). For S = 6 on N = 8, f = (5/6) / (7/8) = 0.952, so less than 5% of the work may stay serial.
Sources of cache incoherence (Hwang): sharing of writable data, process migration from one processor to another, and I/O or DMA that writes memory behind the caches.

concepts.text: Common slips: counting crossbar crosspoints as N + M instead of N × M; forgetting that one 2×2 switch contains four crosspoints; writing hypercube links as n·2^n, which counts every link twice; giving the node count 2^n as the diameter; treating the NUMA remote time as an extra delay on top of the local time; and rounding the bus limit 1/(r·m·t_bus) up instead of down.

formulas.plainText: Amdahl speed-up S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/N), f = parallel fraction, N = processors
Efficiency E = S / N
Hypercube: nodes = 2^n, links = n·2^(n−1), diameter = n

formulas.latex: \text{Crossbar } N\times M:\ N M \text{ crosspoints};\ \text{Omega } N\times N:\ \tfrac{N}{2}\log_2 N \text{ switches}
formulas.plainText: Crossbar N×M: N·M crosspoints; Omega N×N: (N/2)·log2 N switches in log2 N stages

notes.text: Numbers to memorise: 8×8 crossbar = 64 crosspoints; 8×8 omega = 3 stages × 4 switches = 12 switches; 3-cube = 8 nodes, 3 links each, diameter 3; 4-cube = 16 nodes, diameter 4. Amdahl ceiling = 1/(1 − f).

Tightly coupled = shared memory (communication through memory); loosely coupled = private memories (communication by message passing). Do not equate loosely coupled with NUMA: NUMA still has one shared address space, it is just non-uniform in latency.

A crossbar is non-blocking but grows as N×M; a multistage network is cheaper (N/2·log₂N switches) but blocking. The time-shared bus is the cheapest and the least scalable because only one transfer can use it at a time.

formulas.title: Amdahl's law
formulas.description: Speed-up on N processors when only a fraction f of the work is parallelisable; f = 0.9, N = 10 gives 5.26.

formulas.title: Maximum speed-up
formulas.description: The ceiling as the number of processors grows without limit; a 10% serial part caps the speed-up at 10.

formulas.title: Hypercube parameters
formulas.plainText: nodes = 2^n, links = n·2^(n−1), diameter = n
formulas.description: For an n-dimensional binary cube; each node has n neighbours differing in one address bit.

formulas.title: Omega network size
formulas.plainText: stages = log2 N, switches = (N/2)·log2 N
formulas.description: An N×N omega network made of 2×2 interchange switches; 8×8 needs 3 stages and 12 switches.

formulas.title: Parallel efficiency
formulas.plainText: E = S / N
formulas.description: Fraction of the ideal N-fold speed-up actually achieved.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes a tightly coupled from a loosely coupled multiprocessor?
flashcards.back: Tightly coupled processors share a common memory and communicate through it; loosely coupled processors have private memories and communicate by message passing.

flashcards.front: How many stages and 2×2 switches does an 8×8 omega network need?
flashcards.back: log₂8 = 3 stages, each with 8/2 = 4 switches, so 12 switches in total (versus 64 crosspoints for a crossbar).

flashcards.front: State Amdahl's law for N processors.
flashcards.back: S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/N), where f is the parallelisable fraction; the speed-up can never exceed 1/(1 − f).

flashcards.front: In a hypercube, when are two nodes directly connected?
flashcards.back: When their n-bit binary addresses differ in exactly one bit; each node therefore has n neighbours and the diameter is n.

questions.questionText: A hypercube interconnection of dimension 4 has how many processor nodes, and what is the maximum number of hops between any two nodes?
questions.explanation: An n-cube has 2^n nodes and a diameter of n, because two nodes can differ in at most n address bits; for n = 4 that is 16 nodes and 4 hops.

questions.questionText: Which interconnection structure allows every processor to be connected to a different memory module at the same time, at the cost of one switch point for every processor-module pair?
questions.explanation: A crossbar places a switch with arbitration logic at each of the N×M crosspoints, so all combinations of simultaneous, non-blocking connections are possible; the omega network is cheaper but blocking.

questions.questionText: 80% of a program can be executed in parallel and the rest is strictly sequential. According to Amdahl's law, what speed-up is obtained on 4 processors?
questions.explanation: S = 1 / ((1 − 0.8) + 0.8/4) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.2) = 2.5. Even with infinitely many processors the speed-up could not exceed 1/0.2 = 5.

questions.questionText: In Flynn's classification, into which class does a shared-memory multiprocessor fall, given that each of its processors runs its own instruction stream on its own data?
questions.explanation: Multiple processors each executing their own instruction stream on their own data form a multiple-instruction, multiple-data (MIMD) machine. SIMD describes array and vector processors that apply one instruction to many data items.

questions.questionText: According to Mano, which kind of multiprocessor can tolerate a higher degree of interaction between tasks?
options: A cluster of computers linked by a local area network
questions.explanation: Tightly coupled processors exchange data through shared memory quickly, so they cope with frequent interaction; loosely coupled systems, which communicate by messages, are most efficient when interaction between tasks is minimal.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes a multicomputer from a multiprocessor?
options: A multicomputer has several CPUs on one chip sharing a single cache
A multiprocessor has only one CPU but several I/O processors
In a multicomputer each node has private memory and the nodes communicate by message passing, whereas a multiprocessor's CPUs share main memory
In a multicomputer all nodes share one global address space with uniform access time
questions.explanation: A multicomputer is a set of complete computers (processor plus private memory) joined by a network and cooperating by messages; a multiprocessor's processors share one main memory and one operating system.

questions.questionText: One CPU of a multiprocessor fails, yet the system keeps running at reduced performance on the remaining CPUs. Which characteristic of multiprocessors does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Because the processors are interchangeable and share memory and I/O, the failure of one leaves the others able to carry on; this fault tolerance is one of the main benefits of multiprocessors.

questions.questionText: How many crosspoint switches does a crossbar contain if it connects 16 processors to 32 memory modules?
questions.explanation: A crossbar has one crosspoint at every processor–module intersection: 16 × 32 = 512. Adding the counts (48) or squaring either one (256, 1024) is wrong.

questions.questionText: What is the main limitation of a time-shared common bus in a multiprocessor?
options: Every memory module needs a separate port for each processor
It needs N × M crosspoint switches
Processors cannot share any memory over it
Only one processor can transfer over the bus at a time, so contention grows as processors are added
questions.explanation: All units share one path, so while one transfer is in progress every other processor must wait; the bus is the cheapest interconnection but becomes the bottleneck. Separate ports belong to multiport memory and N × M crosspoints to the crossbar.

questions.questionText: In a bus-based multiprocessor each processor keeps the shared bus busy for 15% of the time on average. What is the largest number of processors the bus can support without the total demand exceeding 100%?
questions.explanation: N_max = floor(1 ÷ 0.15) = floor(6.67) = 6; six processors use 90% of the bus while seven would demand 105%. Rounding up to 7 overloads the bus.

questions.questionText: Each processor of a bus-based SMP issues 80 × 10^6 memory references per second and its private cache has a hit ratio of 97.5%. Every miss moves a 32-byte block over a 64-bit bus with a 10 ns bus cycle. Ignoring all other traffic, how many processors can the bus support before it saturates?
questions.explanation: Misses = 80 × 10^6 × 0.025 = 2 × 10^6 per second; bus time per miss = (32 ÷ 8) × 10 ns = 40 ns; one processor uses 2 × 10^6 × 40 ns = 8% of the bus, so floor(1 ÷ 0.08) = floor(12.5) = 12. A 32-bit bus would give 6, and 40 is just 1 ÷ miss ratio.

questions.questionText: In a multiprocessor where every processor has a local bus with its own local memory and I/O, connected through a system bus controller to a common system bus, what is the system bus mainly used for?
options: Reaching the shared memory and communicating with the other processors
Fetching every instruction of every processor
Carrying the local cache's tag comparisons
Connecting the processor to its own local memory
questions.explanation: Local memory and local I/O are reached over the local bus, which keeps most traffic off the common bus; only accesses to the shared memory on the system bus, and hence interprocessor communication, need the system bus.

questions.questionText: A multiport memory system connects 4 processors to 8 memory modules. How many ports does each memory module need, and how many separate processor–module paths are there?
questions.explanation: Every module has one port for each processor, so 4 ports per module, and every processor has its own bus to every module: 4 × 8 = 32 paths. Adding 4 + 8 = 12 counts units, not connections.

questions.questionText: In a multiport memory system, how are simultaneous requests from several processors to the same memory module resolved?
options: By a daisy chain running through all the processors
By the destination tags of an omega network
By the operating system's round-robin scheduler
By fixed priorities assigned to the module's ports
questions.explanation: Mano's multiport memory resolves access conflicts inside each module by giving its ports fixed priorities; the processor on the highest-priority port wins.

questions.questionText: Which interconnection gives each processor its own separate address, data and control buses into every memory module?
questions.explanation: In multiport memory each module has one port per processor, each with its own address, data and control lines; that gives a high transfer rate at the cost of much wiring and control logic.

questions.questionText: According to Mano, what does each crosspoint of a crossbar switch contain?
options: A small cache holding recently used memory words
Multiplexers and arbitration logic that set up the path and resolve simultaneous requests for the same module
A complete processor that forwards messages
Only a fixed wire joining one processor permanently to one module
questions.explanation: Each switch point examines the address on the processor bus to see whether its module is addressed, connects the path through multiplexers and resolves multiple requests for that module on a priority basis.

questions.questionText: A crossbar connects 8 processors to 4 memory modules. What is the maximum number of simultaneous processor–memory transfers, and how many crosspoints does it have?
questions.explanation: Crosspoints = 8 × 4 = 32. Each module can serve only one processor at a time, so at most min(8, 4) = 4 transfers proceed at once, with the other processors waiting.

questions.questionText: How many stages and how many 2×2 switches does a 16×16 omega network need?
questions.explanation: Stages = log₂16 = 4, each with 16 ÷ 2 = 8 switches, so 4 × 8 = 32 switches. 64 counts one switch per line per stage.

questions.questionText: A 64×64 network is built either as a crossbar or as an omega network of 2×2 switches. Counting each 2×2 switch as 4 crosspoints, how many crosspoints does each design need (omega versus crossbar)?
questions.explanation: Omega: log₂64 = 6 stages × 32 switches = 192 switches, × 4 = 768 crosspoints; crossbar: 64 × 64 = 4096. 192 forgets the 4 crosspoints per switch, and 128 counts the crossbar as N + M.

questions.questionText: A 2×2 interchange switch connects its upper input to its lower output and its lower input to its upper output. What is this setting called?
questions.explanation: The four states of a 2×2 switch are straight, exchange (cross), upper broadcast and lower broadcast; swapping the two lines is the exchange state.

questions.questionText: In an 8-line perfect-shuffle connection, to which line is line 6 (binary 110) connected?
questions.explanation: The perfect shuffle rotates the line number left by one bit: 110 becomes 101 = 5. Rotating right gives 011, flipping the last bit (the exchange) gives 111, and shifting left without wrapping the MSB round gives 100.

questions.questionText: In an 8×8 omega network with destination-tag routing (destination bits used from the MSB in stages 1 to 3, 0 = upper output, 1 = lower output), processor 111 requests memory module 011. Which switch outputs does the request take in stages 1, 2 and 3?
questions.explanation: Only the destination 011 matters: bit 0 → upper at stage 1, bit 1 → lower at stage 2, bit 1 → lower at stage 3. Reading the destination from the LSB gives lower, lower, upper, and following the source bits gives lower, lower, lower.

questions.questionText: In an 8×8 omega network (perfect shuffle before each stage, destination-tag routing with the destination bits used from the MSB in stages 1 to 3, 0 = upper output, 1 = lower output), which pair of simultaneous requests cannot both be connected because they need the same link?
questions.explanation: The line after stage i is the source shifted left i places with the first i destination bits shifted in. For P1 (001) → M5 (101) and P3 (011) → M4 (100) the stage-1 lines are 011 and 111, but after stage 2 both are on line 110, so they collide; the other pairs use different lines at every stage.

questions.questionText: Each 2×2 switch of an 8×8 omega network is set either straight or exchange. How many different settings of the whole network are possible, each giving a different permutation of the 8 inputs?
questions.explanation: There are 3 × 4 = 12 switches with 2 settings each, so 2^12 = 4096 permutations, far fewer than the 8! = 40,320 possible ones; 16,777,216 = 4^12 wrongly counts the broadcast states as permutations.

questions.questionText: Which one of these claims about an N×N omega network is false?
options: There is exactly one path from each source to each destination
It is non-blocking, so any permutation of connections can be set up in one pass
Each switch can set itself from one bit of the destination address
questions.explanation: Because the path between a source and a destination is unique and there are only 2^((N/2)log₂N) settings, some request patterns conflict inside the network, so the omega network is blocking. The other statements are true.

questions.questionText: Why is an omega network described as self-routing?
options: Each processor stores a routing table for every possible destination
Messages are flooded to every output and discarded by the wrong modules
Each switch sets itself from one bit of the destination tag carried by the request, so no central controller is needed
The operating system reprograms the switches before every transfer
questions.explanation: At stage i a switch looks at bit i of the destination (counted from the MSB) and chooses its upper output for 0 or its lower output for 1, so the route is fixed by the destination address alone.

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes a single-stage shuffle-exchange network?
options: A crossbar with N × N crosspoints that never blocks
A shared bus on which every processor snoops the others' transfers
A binary n-cube in which each node links to the nodes differing in one bit
One stage of perfect-shuffle wiring followed by exchange switches, through which data recirculate up to log₂N times to reach their destination
questions.explanation: Each pass through the stage rotates the line number left (shuffle) and may flip its last bit (exchange); after log₂N passes every bit of the line number can be set to the destination bit. Unrolling those passes into separate stages gives the omega network.

questions.questionText: A hypercube multicomputer has 128 processors. What is its dimension, and how many links does each node have?
questions.explanation: 2^n = 128 gives n = 7, and a node in an n-cube has one neighbour per address bit, so 7 links. 127 links per node would describe a fully connected network.

questions.questionText: How many communication links does a 6-dimensional hypercube have in total?
questions.explanation: Links = n × 2^(n−1) = 6 × 32 = 192, since each of the 64 nodes has 6 links and each link is shared by two nodes. 384 = 6 × 64 counts every link twice.

questions.questionText: In a 4-dimensional hypercube, what is the minimum number of hops between nodes 0110 and 1011?
questions.explanation: The distance is the number of 1 bits in 0110 XOR 1011 = 1101, which is 3. 5 is the difference of the decimal values 11 − 6, and 4 is the diameter.

questions.questionText: A message travels from node 1010 to node 0111 in a 4-cube using e-cube routing, which corrects the differing address bits starting with the lowest-numbered dimension. Which path does it follow?
questions.explanation: 1010 XOR 0111 = 1101, so dimensions 0, 2 and 3 differ; correcting bit 0, then bit 2, then bit 3 gives 1011, 1111, 0111. The second path corrects the highest dimension first, and the last one changes two bits in one hop, which is not a link.

questions.questionText: In a 5-dimensional hypercube, how many nodes are exactly 2 hops away from a given node?
questions.explanation: A node 2 hops away differs in exactly 2 of the 5 address bits, and there are C(5, 2) = 10 ways to choose them. 20 counts each pair of bits twice (ordered pairs).

questions.questionText: What is the bisection width (number of links cut when the machine is split into two equal halves across one dimension) of a 6-dimensional hypercube?
questions.explanation: Splitting across one dimension leaves two 5-cubes joined by one link per pair of matching nodes: 2^(6−1) = 32 links. 64 is the node count and 192 is the total number of links.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a hypercube (binary n-cube) multiprocessor is NOT correct?
options: All processors share one global memory that they reach through the cube links
Each node has its own local memory and nodes cooperate by message passing
Two nodes are directly linked when their addresses differ in exactly one bit
The diameter grows only as log₂ of the number of nodes
questions.explanation: The hypercube is a loosely coupled structure: each node is a processor with private memory and I/O, and data move between nodes as messages. The other three statements are standard properties of the n-cube.

questions.questionText: How many point-to-point links are needed to connect 12 processors in a fully connected network?
questions.explanation: Each pair of processors needs one link: 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66. 132 counts every link twice, and 11 is the number of links per node.

questions.questionText: How many links does an 8 × 8 two-dimensional mesh without wraparound connections have?
questions.explanation: Each of the 8 rows has 7 horizontal links and each of the 8 columns has 7 vertical links: 2 × 8 × 7 = 112. 128 = 2N is the count for a torus, which adds wraparound links.

questions.questionText: Sixteen processors are connected as a ring, as a 4 × 4 mesh without wraparound, and as a 4-dimensional hypercube. What are the diameters of the three networks, in that order?
questions.explanation: Ring: ⌊16/2⌋ = 8; 4 × 4 mesh: 2(4 − 1) = 6 hops corner to corner; 4-cube: n = 4. 15 is the diameter of a 16-node linear array, and 16 is the hypercube's node count.

questions.questionText: How does a NUMA multiprocessor differ from a UMA multiprocessor?
options: NUMA has no shared address space, so processors exchange messages
In UMA each processor can reach only its own private memory
NUMA is simply another name for a loosely coupled cluster
In NUMA all memories form one shared address space, but a processor reaches remote memory more slowly than its local memory
questions.explanation: Both UMA and NUMA are shared-memory designs; in UMA every word takes the same time from every processor, while in NUMA the latency depends on whether the word is in the processor's own node or a remote one.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a symmetric multiprocessor (SMP) as defined by Stallings?
options: Only one master processor runs the operating system kernel while the others run user tasks as slaves
Two or more similar processors of comparable capability share main memory and I/O
Memory access time is approximately the same for every processor
The system is controlled by a single integrated operating system
questions.explanation: In an SMP all processors can perform the same functions, including running the OS, which is what makes it symmetric; a master–slave arrangement is asymmetric multiprocessing.

questions.questionText: What distinguishes a cache-only memory architecture (COMA)?
options: Each node's local memory acts as a large cache, and data migrate to whichever node uses them without a fixed home location
It has no caches at all, only a central shared memory
Each processor has a private cache but no access to other nodes' memory
Every memory access goes to one global cache shared over a bus
questions.explanation: In COMA the distributed memories behave as attraction memories: a block is not tied to one home node but moves to and is replicated in the nodes that reference it.

questions.questionText: In a NUMA multiprocessor a local memory access takes 100 ns and a remote access 400 ns. If 80% of a program's references are local, what is its average memory access time?
questions.explanation: t_avg = 0.8 × 100 + 0.2 × 400 = 80 + 80 = 160 ns. 250 ns is the plain average, 340 ns swaps the fractions, and 180 ns wrongly adds the local time to every remote access.

questions.questionText: On a NUMA machine a local access takes 100 ns and a remote access 600 ns. What minimum fraction of references must be local for the average access time to be no more than 150 ns?
questions.explanation: 100p + 600(1 − p) ≤ 150 gives 600 − 500p ≤ 150, so p ≥ 450 ÷ 500 = 0.9 = 90%. 10% is the largest remote fraction allowed, not the local one.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the cache coherence problem is correct?
options: Coherence problems arise only with write-through caches
Coherence is guaranteed if all caches use the same block size
A write-back cache cannot cause coherence problems because memory is updated later
Write-through keeps main memory up to date, but other caches may still hold the old value, so write-through alone does not ensure coherence
questions.explanation: With write-through the writer's cache and memory are consistent, but copies in other processors' caches are not updated; with write-back even memory is stale. Some protocol, such as snooping or a directory, is needed in both cases.

questions.questionText: Memory location X holds 10. Processors P1 and P2 each read X into their private write-back caches, and there is no coherence protocol. P1 then writes 15 to X, after which P2 reads X again. What does P2 read, and what does main memory hold at that moment?
options: P2 reads 15 from P1's cache, and memory holds 10
P2 reads 10 from its own cache, and memory still holds 10
questions.explanation: P1's write-back cache updates only its own copy (now dirty), so memory keeps 10 until that line is evicted, and P2 hits on its stale copy of 10. Memory would hold 15 only with write-through, and P2 would see 15 only if a coherence protocol invalidated or updated its copy.

questions.questionText: Which of the following does NOT cause a cache coherence problem in a shared-memory multiprocessor?
options: Two processors writing to the same shared variable
A process migrating from one processor to another
Several processors reading the same read-only program code
A DMA device writing memory behind the caches
questions.explanation: Coherence problems come from sharing writable data, process migration and I/O that modifies memory; copies of read-only code are never written, so they always stay identical.

questions.questionText: 5% of a program is strictly sequential and the rest parallelises perfectly. According to Amdahl's law, what is the maximum speed-up obtainable with any number of processors?
questions.explanation: As N grows without limit, S = 1 ÷ ((1 − f) + f/N) approaches 1 ÷ (1 − f) = 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20. 1.05 is 1 ÷ 0.95, which inverts the parallel fraction instead of the serial one.

questions.questionText: A program is 90% parallelisable. According to Amdahl's law, what is the parallel efficiency when it runs on 8 processors?
questions.explanation: S = 1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.9/8) = 1 ÷ 0.2125 = 4.71, so E = S/N = 4.71 ÷ 8 = 58.8%. 91.3% comes from the scaled (Gustafson) speed-up 0.1 + 0.9 × 8 = 7.3, and 13.7% from swapping the serial and parallel parts.

questions.questionText: What fraction of a program must be parallelisable for it to reach a speed-up of 12 on 16 processors, according to Amdahl's law?
Which statement about Amdahl's law is NOT correct?
options: The speed-up can never exceed 1/(1 − f), however many processors are used
If the whole program is parallelisable (f = 1), the speed-up equals N
Parallel efficiency S/N always increases as more processors are added
A small serial fraction severely limits the speed-up on large machines
questions.explanation: For f < 1, S grows more slowly than N, so the efficiency S/N falls as processors are added; for example with f = 0.9 it drops from 0.53 at N = 10 to 0.09 at N = 100. The other statements follow directly from S = 1 ÷ ((1 − f) + f/N).

subtopics.title: Inter-processor Communication & Synchronization
subtopics.subtitle: Shared memory vs messages, semaphores, test-and-set, bus arbitration, cache coherence

concepts.text: How Processors Communicate

In a shared-memory (tightly coupled) multiprocessor the common memory is the communication medium. A processor that wants to send information writes it into a shared memory area that the operating system reserves for this purpose; the receiver reads it. Each processor may be assigned a mailbox, a memory area holding messages addressed to it, and the sender simply deposits the message there. The receiver must learn that a message has arrived: it can periodically inspect its mailbox (polling of memory), or the sender can raise an interprocessor interrupt, a signal that one processor sends over the bus to a specific other processor to notify it of an event or of a pending message.
Communication mechanisms, from tightly to loosely coupled:
items: Shared variables in common memory: fastest; the operating system allocates the area and processors use ordinary load/store instructions. Needs synchronization to avoid corrupting shared data.
Mailbox: a dedicated memory area per processor plus a status flag; the sender writes the message and sets the flag, the receiver clears it after reading.

Interprocessor interrupt: a processor writes to an interrupt register of the target processor (or uses a dedicated line), forcing it to run a handler; used to deliver urgent events and to start the operating system's scheduler on another CPU.

Message passing (loosely coupled): each node has private memory; information is packaged into packets and sent over communication channels (point-to-point links, a switching network or a LAN). The sending node does not wait; the packet is routed through intermediate nodes to its destination.
Shared I/O and shared operating system data: the OS also keeps a process table and other structures in shared memory that all processors must access consistently.

concepts.text: Why Synchronization Is Needed

Processors that share data must coordinate their accesses in time, which is called synchronization. A critical section is a program segment that accesses a shared resource and must be completed by one processor before any other processor may begin a section that touches the same resource. If two processors execute read-modify-write sequences on the same variable at the same time, the result depends on the exact timing (a race condition) and can be wrong: two processors each incrementing a shared counter can leave it incremented once. The property that only one processor at a time executes a critical section is mutual exclusion.
Mutual exclusion with a semaphore:
items: A binary semaphore is a variable in shared memory that indicates whether a resource is in use: 1 = busy (a processor is in the critical section), 0 = free.
Before entering a critical section a processor tests the semaphore; if it is 0 it sets it to 1 and enters; if it is 1 it waits and retries. On leaving it resets the semaphore to 0.
The test and the set must be a single indivisible operation. If processor A reads 0 and, before it writes 1, processor B also reads 0, both enter the critical section and mutual exclusion is broken.
Counting semaphores extend this to resources with several instances; higher-level constructs (locks, mutexes, monitors) are built on the same primitive.

concepts.text: Hardware support is the test-and-set instruction (TSL SEM in Mano's treatment). In one indivisible read-modify-write memory cycle it copies the current value of the semaphore into a processor flag and writes 1 into the semaphore: SEM → F, 1 → SEM. To make the cycle indivisible the processor asserts a bus lock signal that prevents any other processor from taking the bus between the read and the write. After TSL the processor examines F: F = 0 means the semaphore was free and is now taken, so it proceeds; F = 1 means it was already busy, so the processor loops and tries again (a spin lock or busy wait). Other atomic primitives serve the same purpose: swap (exchange), fetch-and-add, compare-and-swap.

concepts.latex: \text{TSL SEM}:\ SEM \rightarrow F,\ 1 \rightarrow SEM\ (\text{one locked bus cycle})
concepts.plainText: TSL SEM: copy SEM to flag F, then set SEM = 1, in one indivisible bus-locked cycle

concepts.text: Other synchronization mechanisms:
items: Barrier: a point that every participating processor must reach before any may continue; implemented with a shared counter that each arrival increments atomically and a flag released when the count equals the number of processors. Used between phases of a parallel algorithm.
Event flags and condition variables: a processor waits until another sets a flag, avoiding continuous polling when combined with interrupts.

Deadlock: two or more processors wait forever for resources held by each other. It requires four conditions at once — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait — and is handled by prevention (break one condition, e.g. acquire locks in a fixed order), avoidance, or detection and recovery.

concepts.text: Interprocessor Arbitration

Processors, memory and I/O of a tightly coupled system share a system bus (Mano's example has 86 lines: 16 data, 24 address, control and arbitration lines). When several processors request the bus at the same time, arbitration logic decides which becomes the bus master; the others wait. Arbitration is either static (priorities fixed by hardware) or dynamic (priorities change during execution to be fair).

rows: Bus-grant line passes through the arbiters PI → PO; the first requesting unit blocks it and takes the bus when the bus-busy line is free
Fixed by position; nearest the arbiter is highest
Simplest; few lines; slow for long chains; cannot be changed
Each unit has a request line into a priority encoder; a decoder returns the grant on the selected line
Faster than daisy chain; one line per unit
The bus is allotted to each processor for a fixed interval in round-robin order
The arbiter puts a processor number on poll lines; the addressed processor takes the bus if it has a request; the sequence can be programmed
Highest priority to the unit that has not used the bus for the longest time
Requests queued in order of arrival; the earliest is served first
Like the daisy chain but the highest priority moves to the unit after the one that last held the bus
Fair version of the daisy chain

concepts.text: Cache Coherence Solutions
Ways of keeping private caches consistent in a shared-memory system:
items: No private caches for shared data: a single shared cache, or shared writable data marked non-cacheable so that all such accesses go to main memory; simple but slow.
Write-through with software control: the compiler or OS marks which data are shared and read-only (cacheable) versus shared and writable (non-cacheable) or flushes caches at critical points.

Snoopy (bus-watching) protocols: each cache controller monitors the shared bus for writes to lines it holds. Write-invalidate (MESI: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) invalidates other copies before a write so one cache owns the line; write-update (write-broadcast) instead sends the new data to every cache holding the line. Suits bus-based UMA systems.

Directory-based protocols: a directory in memory (or distributed with each memory module) records which caches hold each line; a write consults the directory and sends invalidations only to those caches, avoiding bus broadcasts. Used in scalable NUMA systems with point-to-point interconnects.
Synchronization primitives interact with coherence: the bus lock during test-and-set guarantees that the semaphore read and write are seen by all processors as one atomic action.

rows: On a write to a shared line
In every cache; all watch the bus
Other copies invalidated; writer gets Modified state
In every cache; all watch the bus
New value broadcast to all caches holding the line
Data written and then read by many processors
Central or distributed directory in memory
Directory sends invalidations only to listed sharers
Large NUMA systems with switched interconnects

concepts.text: Putting it together: a tightly coupled multiprocessor needs three layers of coordination. Arbitration decides who may use the bus in the next cycle; cache coherence guarantees that every processor sees the same value for a memory word; synchronization (semaphores built on test-and-set, barriers) guarantees that critical sections of the software run one at a time. MCQs on this subtopic mostly ask for the indivisibility of test-and-set, the meaning of the semaphore values, the name of an arbitration algorithm from its description, and snoopy versus directory coherence.
Going Deeper: MESI, Lock Traffic and Bus Contention

MESI is the write-invalidate snooping protocol used with write-back caches in many bus-based multiprocessors; every cache line carries one of four states. Modified (M) means the line is valid only in this cache and has been written, so main memory is stale and this cache must supply or write back the data before anyone else uses it. Exclusive (E) means only this cache holds the line and it equals memory; Shared (S) means other caches may also hold it and all copies equal memory; Invalid (I) means the line holds nothing usable. The E state is what MESI adds to a three-state MSI protocol: a processor that reads private data and later writes it moves E to M silently, with no bus transaction.

rows: Another cache wants to write (snooped RWITM or invalidate)
Read or write hit; stays M, no bus traffic
Supplies the line and writes it back to memory; goes to S
Writes the line back to memory; goes to I
Read hit stays E; write hit goes to M with no bus traffic
Read hit stays S; write hit sends an invalidate and goes to M
Read miss: BusRd, loads E if no other cache has the line, else S. Write miss: RWITM, loads M

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: MESI trace, three write-back caches, X starts in memory only
Step Access       Bus action                          P1 P2 P3
1    P1 reads X   BusRd, no other copy                E  I  I
2    P2 reads X   BusRd, P1 E -> S                    S  S  I
3    P1 writes X  Invalidate, P2 S -> I               M  I  I
4    P3 reads X   BusRd, P1 writes X back, M -> S     S  I  S
5    P2 writes X  RWITM, P1 and P3 S -> I             I  M  I
6    P2 reads X   Hit, no bus action                  I  M  I
Bus transactions = 3 BusRd + 1 invalidate + 1 RWITM = 5
Write-backs = 1 (step 4); memory is stale again after step 5

Write-update protocols such as Dragon and Firefly keep every copy valid by broadcasting each written word, so a consumer that reads right after a write hits in its own cache; but a processor that writes the same line many times sends one broadcast per write even when nobody reads in between. Write-invalidate pays one invalidation for the first write and then writes locally, while every other processor that later reads the line takes a miss. Because runs of writes to the same line without intervening reads by others are common, most commercial processors use write-invalidate (MESI and variants such as MOESI and MESIF). False sharing is its pathological case: two processors write different words that happen to lie in one line, so the line ping-pongs between their caches although no data is really shared, and padding the variables into separate lines cures it.
Spin locks and atomic primitives on a snooping bus:
items: Plain test-and-set spinning: every retry is an atomic read-modify-write that needs the line in the Modified state, so each attempt is a bus transaction; k waiters retrying every t seconds cause k/t transactions per second while the lock stays busy, slowing even the lock holder's own memory traffic.

Test-and-test-and-set: a waiter first reads the lock with an ordinary load; after one read miss it spins on its Shared cached copy with no bus traffic and issues test-and-set only when it sees 0. The release write invalidates all copies and causes one short burst of misses.
Exponential backoff: after a failed attempt a waiter delays for a growing random time before retrying, trading a little latency for much less contention.
Compare-and-swap CAS(addr, expected, new): writes new only if M[addr] equals expected and always returns the old value, so a failed CAS leaves memory unchanged and tells the caller what it found.
Fetch-and-add FAA(addr, k): returns the old value and adds k indivisibly; n processors each doing FAA(c, 1) receive n different values, the basis of ticket locks and barrier counters.

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: how many processors can one shared bus carry?
Each processor: 10^8 memory references/s, hit ratio 0.97 in its private cache
Every miss holds the bus for 40 ns (address plus block transfer)
Bus requests per processor = 10^8 x (1 - 0.97) = 3 x 10^6 per second
Bus share per processor    = 3 x 10^6 x 40 ns = 0.12 (12 % of bus time)
Saturation: N x 0.12 <= 1  ->  N <= 8.33, so at most 8 processors
With 6 processors U = 6 x 0.12 = 0.72; waiting time rises steeply as U -> 1

concepts.plainText: Bus utilisation U = N × r × t_b must stay ≤ 1, so N_max = floor(1 / (r × t_b)); r = bus transactions per second per processor, t_b = bus time per transaction

concepts.text: A directory protocol replaces broadcasting with bookkeeping. In a full-map directory every memory block has an entry with one presence bit per processor and a dirty bit, plus a state such as Uncached, Shared or Exclusive; on a write the home node sends invalidations only to the processors whose bits are set and records the writer as the owner. Because the entry grows with N, large machines use limited-pointer directories that store a few processor numbers of log2 N bits each, or chain the sharers in a linked list kept in the caches, as the SCI standard does.

concepts.plainText: Full-map directory: N presence bits + 1 dirty bit per memory block of B bytes; storage overhead = (N + 1)/(8B)

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: size of a full-map directory
Memory 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes, block B = 64 bytes, N = 32 processors
Blocks          = 2^30 / 2^6 = 2^24 = 16,777,216
Bits per entry  = 32 presence bits + 1 dirty bit = 33
Directory size  = 33 x 2^24 bits = 33 x 2^21 bytes = 66 MiB
Overhead        = 33 / (64 x 8) = 6.4 % of main memory
Limited pointers (4 x log2 32 + 1 = 21 bits) would need 42 MiB

Common slips in these problems: an E line changes to M on a local write without any bus transaction, but an S line must first broadcast an invalidate; a read miss loads E only when no other cache holds the line; a snooped read of an M line forces a write-back and leaves both copies Shared. When sizing a directory, remember the dirty bit and convert bits to bytes.

formulas.plainText: Test-and-set: SEM → F, then 1 → SEM, indivisibly
Links to connect N nodes fully = N(N − 1)/2
Time-slice arbitration: each of N processors gets T_round / N of the bus per round
Speed-up with synchronization overhead: S = T1 / (T1/N + T_sync)

notes.text: Test-and-set must be indivisible (one read-modify-write cycle with the bus locked). In Mano's convention semaphore = 1 means the resource is busy and 0 means free; after TSL, flag F = 0 means you got the resource.

Do not mix up the two daisy chains: the interrupt daisy chain passes interrupt acknowledge, the arbitration daisy chain passes bus grant. Both give the unit nearest the source the highest fixed priority; only the rotating daisy chain makes it fair.
Snoopy protocols need a broadcast medium (a bus) so every cache can listen; directory protocols work over point-to-point networks and therefore scale to large NUMA machines.

Dynamic arbitration keywords: fixed interval in turn = time slice; arbiter addresses each unit = polling; longest idle wins = LRU; earliest request wins = FIFO; priority moves to the unit after the last master = rotating daisy chain.

formulas.title: Test-and-set semantics
formulas.plainText: SEM → F; 1 → SEM (one indivisible cycle)
formulas.description: The old semaphore value is copied into flag F and the semaphore is set to 1 without releasing the bus in between.

formulas.title: Fully connected links
formulas.description: Number of point-to-point links needed to connect every pair of N nodes directly; 8 nodes need 28 links.

formulas.title: Time-slice bus share
formulas.plainText: T_slice = T_round / N
formulas.description: In time-slice arbitration each of N processors owns the bus for an equal fixed interval per round.

formulas.title: Speed-up with synchronization cost
formulas.plainText: S = T1 / (T1/N + T_sync)
formulas.description: Lock, barrier and communication time T_sync added to the ideal T1/N reduces the achievable speed-up.

flashcards.back: A program segment that accesses a shared resource and must be completed by one processor before another processor may execute a section that uses the same resource.

flashcards.front: What does the test-and-set instruction TSL SEM do, and why is it hardware-supported?
flashcards.back: It copies SEM into a flag and sets SEM to 1 in one indivisible bus-locked cycle, so no other processor can read the old value in between; this is what makes a semaphore reliable.

flashcards.front: List the dynamic bus arbitration algorithms.
flashcards.back: Time slice, polling, least recently used (LRU), first-in first-out (FIFO) and rotating daisy chain.

flashcards.front: Snoopy vs directory-based cache coherence: what is the key difference?
flashcards.back: Snoopy caches watch a shared bus for writes (broadcast); directory protocols keep a record of which caches hold each line and send invalidations point-to-point, scaling to large systems.

questions.questionText: Why must the test-and-set instruction used for a semaphore be executed as an indivisible read-modify-write cycle?
options: So that the semaphore can be stored in a processor register instead of memory
So that the instruction executes faster than a normal memory write
So that no other processor can read the semaphore between its test and its update, which would let two processors enter the critical section
So that the interrupt system is disabled for the whole critical section
questions.explanation: If another processor could access the semaphore between the read and the write, both could see it as free and both would set it, breaking mutual exclusion; the bus is locked for the duration of the instruction to prevent this.

questions.questionText: In a loosely coupled multiprocessor, inter-processor communication is achieved mainly through
options: shared variables in a common global memory
message passing over a communication network
a common cache shared by all processors
questions.explanation: Loosely coupled processors have private memories and no global shared memory, so they exchange information as packets (messages) routed over links or a switching network.

questions.questionText: Which dynamic bus arbitration algorithm allots the bus to each processor for a fixed-length interval in a round-robin sequence, regardless of whether it needs the bus?
questions.explanation: Time-slice arbitration divides bus time into equal fixed slots given to each processor in turn; FIFO serves by arrival, LRU favours the longest-idle unit and the rotating daisy chain moves the top priority after each use.

questions.questionText: A snoopy cache coherence protocol relies on which mechanism?
options: Every cache controller monitoring the shared bus for writes to lines it holds
A central directory in memory that lists which caches hold each line
Marking all shared data as non-cacheable
Flushing every cache at each context switch
questions.explanation: Snoopy protocols (write-invalidate such as MESI, or write-update) work because every cache watches the broadcast bus and reacts to writes from other processors; the directory approach is the alternative for non-bus interconnects.

questions.questionText: In a shared-memory multiprocessor, a sending processor places a request for another processor in a reserved area of common memory, with status bits showing whether the area holds a message and for which processor it is meant. What is this area called?
questions.explanation: Mano calls this memory area a mailbox: the sender writes the message and the status bits, and the receiver checks it by polling or after an interprocessor interrupt. A directory entry records cached copies of a block, not messages.

questions.questionText: A processor has just left a message in the mailbox of processor P3 and wants P3 to handle it immediately rather than at its next periodic check of the mailbox. What should it use?
options: A DMA transfer from its own cache to P3's cache
An interprocessor interrupt directed to P3
A bus request at the highest arbitration priority
A cache flush of the mailbox line
questions.explanation: An interprocessor interrupt forces the target processor to run a handler at once, so it need not poll its mailbox; bus arbitration only decides who uses the bus next.

questions.questionText: Which is an advantage of communicating through shared memory rather than by message passing?
options: Processors exchange data with ordinary load and store instructions, without packaging and routing messages
No synchronization between the processors is ever needed
It scales more easily to thousands of processors
Each processor can keep all of its data private
questions.explanation: Shared variables are read and written directly, which is fast and simple to program. The price is the need for locks and cache coherence and limited scalability, where message passing over a network is stronger.

questions.questionText: In which multiprocessor operating-system organisation does one designated processor always execute the operating-system functions, while the others only run user programs and must ask it for OS services?
options: Separate operating system for each processor
questions.explanation: Mano lists three organisations: master-slave (one processor runs the OS), separate OS (each processor has its own copy, suited to loosely coupled systems) and distributed OS, where OS routines float from processor to processor but each function runs on only one at a time.

questions.questionText: A node of a message-passing multiprocessor sends a 4,000-byte message to a neighbour. The software start-up time is 20 µs and the link bandwidth is 50 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes). How long does the transfer take?
questions.explanation: T = t_startup + L/B = 20 µs + 4,000 B / (50 × 10^6 B/s) = 20 + 80 = 100 µs. Leaving out the start-up gives 80 µs, and misreading 50 MB/s as 50 Mbit/s gives 20 + 640 = 660 µs.

questions.questionText: A 2,000-byte message crosses 4 links (hops) of a message-passing network, each with a bandwidth of 100 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes); ignore start-up time. With store-and-forward routing each node receives the whole message before forwarding it; with cut-through routing only a header delay of 0.2 µs is added per hop. What are the two transfer times?
options: 80 µs with store-and-forward, 20.8 µs with cut-through
20 µs with store-and-forward, 20.8 µs with cut-through
80 µs with store-and-forward, 80.8 µs with cut-through
640 µs with store-and-forward, 160.8 µs with cut-through
questions.explanation: One link transmission takes 2,000 / 10^8 = 20 µs. Store-and-forward repeats it on every link: 4 × 20 = 80 µs; cut-through pipelines the message through the nodes: 20 + 4 × 0.2 = 20.8 µs.

questions.questionText: Two processors update the same shared variable with separate load, modify and store instructions, and the final value depends on how their instructions happen to interleave in time. What is this situation called?
questions.explanation: When the outcome of unsynchronised read-modify-write sequences depends on timing it is a race condition; putting the update in a critical section protected by a lock removes it.

questions.questionText: A shared counter holds 5. Processors P1 and P2 each execute the sequence LOAD R, count; ADD R, 1; STORE count, R exactly once, without any lock. Which final values of count are possible?
questions.explanation: If the two sequences do not overlap the result is 7; if both load 5 before either stores, both store 6 and one increment is lost. The value cannot stay 5 because at least one store of 6 or 7 always happens.

questions.questionText: Processor P1 executes Mano's test-and-set instruction TSL SEM, which leaves the tested (old) value of SEM in processor register R, while SEM = 0 (Mano's convention: 0 = resource free, 1 = busy). What are SEM and R afterwards, and what does P1 do?
options: SEM = 1, R = 0; P1 enters the critical section
SEM = 1, R = 1; P1 waits and retries
SEM = 0, R = 1; P1 enters the critical section
SEM = 0, R = 0; P1 waits and retries
questions.explanation: TSL performs R ← M[SEM] and M[SEM] ← 1 in one locked operation, so R receives the old value 0 and SEM becomes 1. R = 0 tells P1 that the resource was free and now belongs to it, so it enters the critical section; R = 1 would mean another processor holds it.

questions.questionText: In Mano's description of semaphores in a multiprocessor, what is the hardware lock?
options: A processor-generated signal that prevents other processors from using the system bus while it is active
A bit in each cache line that stops the line from being replaced
A key register that must match before a processor may write to memory
A watchdog timer that aborts a critical section that runs too long
questions.explanation: The hardware lock is asserted while the test-and-set instruction executes, so no other processor can take the bus between the read and the write of the semaphore.

questions.questionText: A counting semaphore S with initial value 2 guards two identical printers. wait(S) decrements S and blocks the caller if the result is negative; signal(S) increments S and wakes one blocked process if the result is 0 or less, so a negative S equals minus the number of blocked processes. The processes perform, in order: wait, wait, wait, wait, signal, wait, signal. What is S at the end, and how many processes are blocked?
questions.explanation: S goes 2 → 1 → 0 → −1 → −2 (two blocked), then signal gives −1 (one woken), wait gives −2 and the last signal gives −1. One process is still waiting for a printer.

questions.questionText: The atomic instruction CAS(addr, expected, new) writes new into M[addr] only if M[addr] equals expected, and always returns the old value of M[addr]. M[addr] = 7 and a processor executes CAS(addr, 5, 9). What happens?
options: It returns 7 and M[addr] stays 7, so the update has failed
questions.explanation: The comparison 7 = 5 fails, so memory is not changed and the caller receives the current value 7; it would normally retry with 7 as the new expected value.

questions.questionText: A shared counter c = 10. Three processors each execute the atomic fetch-and-add FAA(c, 1), which returns the old value of c and adds 1 to it. Which outcome is guaranteed?
options: All three receive 10 and c ends at 11
All three receive 10 and c ends at 13
The processors receive 10, 11 and 12 in some order, and c ends at 13
The values received depend on timing, and c may end at 11, 12 or 13
questions.explanation: Each FAA is indivisible, so the three updates are serialised: every caller receives a different old value and no increment is lost, whatever the order.

questions.questionText: Which synchronization mechanism makes each processor wait at a given point of a parallel program until every participating processor has reached that point?
options: A binary semaphore guarding a critical section
questions.explanation: A barrier is usually a shared counter incremented atomically by each arrival plus a release flag set when the count reaches the number of processors; it separates phases of a parallel algorithm.

questions.questionText: With fixed-priority daisy-chain bus arbitration, the processor at the far end of the chain may wait indefinitely because processors nearer the arbiter keep requesting the bus. What is this problem called?
questions.explanation: No rule forbids the low-priority unit from using the bus, yet it is postponed indefinitely: that is starvation. Dynamic schemes such as the rotating daisy chain, LRU or FIFO arbitration prevent it.

questions.questionText: Processor A holds lock L1 and waits for L2, while processor B holds L2 and waits for L1. Which rule, applied to all code, prevents this situation?
options: Every processor releases its lock as soon as it is granted the bus
Locks are implemented with test-and-test-and-set instead of test-and-set
Every processor acquires the locks in one fixed global order, for example L1 before L2
Each processor waits with exponential backoff before retrying
questions.explanation: A fixed acquisition order makes circular wait impossible, and circular wait is one of the four conditions needed for deadlock. The spin-lock refinements only reduce bus traffic.

questions.questionText: Why does a test-and-test-and-set spin lock produce far less bus traffic than one that simply repeats the test-and-set instruction?
options: It locks the bus for the whole time the lock is held, so no other traffic can occur
It keeps the lock in a processor register instead of memory
Waiting processors spin by reading their cached Shared copy of the lock and attempt the atomic test-and-set only when they see it free
It lets several processors enter the critical section together, so fewer have to wait
questions.explanation: Every test-and-set is a read-modify-write that needs exclusive ownership of the line, so repeating it keeps generating bus transactions. Ordinary reads hit in the local cache until the holder's release write invalidates the copies.

questions.questionText: Processor P0 holds a spin lock for 2 µs while 4 other processors wait for it. With plain test-and-set, each waiter retries every 100 ns and every retry is one bus transaction. With test-and-test-and-set, each waiter takes one read miss to load the lock line and then spins in its own cache. How many bus transactions do the waiters cause while P0 holds the lock?
questions.explanation: Test-and-set: 2 µs / 100 ns = 20 retries per waiter, 4 × 20 = 80 transactions. Test-and-test-and-set: one read miss per waiter, 4 transactions, then local cache hits until the release.

questions.questionText: Each iteration of a parallel loop spends 40 µs on private work and then 10 µs in a critical section protected by one lock. Ignoring lock overhead, what is the maximum total throughput with any number of processors, and at how many processors is that bound first reached?
questions.explanation: Only one processor can be in the critical section at a time, so at most 1 / 10 µs = 100,000 iterations/s. One processor alone completes 1 / 50 µs = 20,000 iterations/s, so 100,000 / 20,000 = 5 processors saturate the lock.

questions.questionText: A job takes 800 ms on one processor. On 8 processors the work divides perfectly, but lock and barrier waiting adds 20 ms. Using S = T1 / (T1/N + T_sync), what is the speed-up?
questions.explanation: S = 800 / (800/8 + 20) = 800 / 120 = 6.67. Ignoring T_sync gives the ideal 8, and 8 × 800/820 = 7.80 wrongly adds the overhead to the one-processor time.

questions.questionText: Eight processors share a bus under time-slice arbitration, with 50 ns slots given in a fixed round-robin order whether or not a processor needs the bus. A processor needs the bus immediately after its own slot has ended. How long must it wait for its next slot to begin?
questions.explanation: The slots of the other seven processors come first, each 50 ns long even if they are idle: 7 × 50 = 350 ns. 400 ns is the full round including its own slot.

questions.questionText: Four processors are connected in a rotating daisy chain in the order P0 → P1 → P2 → P3 → back to P0. P1 has just released the bus, and P0 and P3 now request it at the same time. Which processor gets the bus, and which processor has the lowest priority in this arbitration?
options: P0 gets the bus; P3 has the lowest priority
P0 gets the bus; P1 has the lowest priority
P3 gets the bus; P0 has the lowest priority
P3 gets the bus; P1 has the lowest priority
questions.explanation: In a rotating daisy chain the priority order starts at the unit after the last bus master: P2, P3, P0, P1. P2 is not requesting, so P3 wins, and P1, which just used the bus, is last; a fixed daisy chain would have chosen P0.

questions.questionText: Six processors share a bus. Each generates 2.5 × 10^6 bus transactions per second, and every transaction occupies the bus for 40 ns. What is the bus utilisation?
questions.explanation: One processor uses 2.5 × 10^6 × 40 × 10^-9 = 0.10 of the bus time, so six use 6 × 0.10 = 0.60, that is 60 %.

questions.questionText: Each processor in a bus-based multiprocessor keeps the shared bus busy 8 % of the time when running alone. Ignoring queueing effects, what is the largest number of processors whose total bus demand does not exceed 100 %?
questions.explanation: N × 0.08 ≤ 1 gives N ≤ 12.5, so 12 processors (96 %); a 13th would demand 104 % of the bus.

questions.questionText: Each processor issues 2 × 10^8 memory references per second, and 98.5 % of them hit in its private cache. Every miss occupies the shared bus for 25 ns. What fraction of bus time does one processor use, and what is the largest number of processors whose total demand does not exceed the bus capacity?
questions.explanation: Misses = 2 × 10^8 × 0.015 = 3 × 10^6 per second; bus share = 3 × 10^6 × 25 ns = 0.075. Then N ≤ 1/0.075 = 13.3, so 13 processors; 14 would need 105 % of the bus.

questions.questionText: In each bus cycle, each of 4 processors independently requests the bus with probability 0.3. What is the probability that two or more processors request in the same cycle, so that arbitration must make at least one of them wait?
questions.explanation: P(no request) = 0.7^4 = 0.2401 and P(exactly one) = 4 × 0.3 × 0.7^3 = 0.4116, so P(two or more) = 1 − 0.2401 − 0.4116 = 0.348. 0.760 is the probability of at least one request.

questions.questionText: In the MESI protocol, which state means that the line is valid only in this cache and has been written, so the copy in main memory is out of date?
questions.explanation: Modified means dirty and exclusive: the cache must write the line back, or supply it, before anyone else uses it. An Exclusive line is also the only cached copy, but it still equals memory.

questions.questionText: Under MESI, processor P1 read-misses on block X and no other cache holds X. In which state is X loaded into P1's cache?
questions.explanation: No other cache responds to the snoop, so this is the only cached copy and it equals memory: Exclusive. If another cache had held X, both copies would end up Shared.

questions.questionText: Which MESI state change takes place without any transaction on the shared bus?
options: Shared to Modified when the local processor writes the line
Exclusive to Modified when the local processor writes the line
Invalid to Exclusive when the local processor reads the line
Invalid to Modified when the local processor writes the line
questions.explanation: A line in E is known to be the only cached copy, so the write needs nobody's permission. S to M must broadcast an invalidate, and both transitions out of I need a bus read (BusRd or read-with-intent-to-modify).

questions.questionText: Cache C2 holds block X in the Modified state. Processor P1 then read-misses on X. With the MESI protocol as described by Stallings, what happens?
options: C2 supplies X and writes it back to memory, then changes to Shared; P1 loads X as Shared
C2 keeps X as Modified and P1 reads the stale value from memory
C2 invalidates its copy and P1 loads X as Exclusive
C2 changes to Exclusive and P1 loads X as Modified
questions.explanation: The snooping C2 must not let P1 read stale memory, so it provides the dirty line, memory is updated, and both caches end with clean Shared copies.

questions.questionText: Caches C1 and C3 hold block Y in the Shared state. Processor P2, whose cache does not contain Y, writes to Y. Under MESI, what are the states of Y in C1, C2 and C3 afterwards?
questions.explanation: P2's write miss issues a read-with-intent-to-modify; C1 and C3 snoop it and invalidate their copies, and P2 loads the line and writes it, so only C2 holds Y, in Modified.

questions.questionText: Three processors have write-back MESI caches, and block X is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P1 reads X, P2 reads X, P3 writes X, P1 reads X. What are the final states of X in the caches of P1, P2 and P3? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
questions.explanation: P1 loads E; P2's read makes both S; P3's write miss (RWITM) invalidates P1 and P2 and leaves P3 in M; P1's read miss makes P3 write X back and drop to S, and P1 loads S.

questions.questionText: Two processors have write-back MESI caches, and block A is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P1 reads A, P1 writes A, P1 writes A, P2 reads A, P2 writes A. Counting each read miss (BusRd), read-with-intent-to-modify and invalidate as one bus transaction, and write-backs separately, how many bus transactions and write-backs occur? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
questions.explanation: P1's read is a BusRd (E); its two writes are silent (E to M, then an M hit); P2's read is a BusRd that makes P1 write back and go to S; P2's write is an invalidate (S to M). That is 3 transactions and 1 write-back.

questions.questionText: Three processors have write-back MESI caches, and block X is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P1 writes X, P2 reads X, P3 reads X, P3 writes X, P1 reads X, P2 writes X. Counting each BusRd, read-with-intent-to-modify and invalidate as one bus transaction, how many bus transactions and write-backs occur, and what is the final state of X in P2's cache? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
options: 6 bus transactions, 1 write-back; P2 holds X as Modified
6 bus transactions, 2 write-backs; P2 holds X as Modified
5 bus transactions, 2 write-backs; P2 holds X as Exclusive
6 bus transactions, 3 write-backs; P2 holds X as Shared
questions.explanation: Steps: RWITM (P1 M); BusRd with P1 writing back (P1, P2 S); BusRd (all S); invalidate (P3 M); BusRd with P3 writing back (P1, P3 S); RWITM (P2 M, others I). Every access uses the bus once, giving 6 transactions and 2 write-backs.

questions.questionText: Three processors have write-back MESI caches, and block X is initially only in memory. The accesses are: P2 reads X, P1 reads X, P2 writes X, P2 writes X, P3 writes X, P1 reads X, P3 reads X. What are the final states of X in P1, P2 and P3, and how many times is X written back to memory? Assume Stallings' MESI rules: a read miss loads E only if no other cache holds the block, otherwise S; a cache that snoops another processor's read of its M block writes it back to memory and changes to S; a snooped read-with-intent-to-modify or invalidate makes every other copy I, an M copy being written back first.
questions.explanation: P2 E; P1 read makes both S; P2's first write invalidates P1 (P2 M) and the second hits; P3's write miss makes P2 write back and go to I (P3 M); P1's read makes P3 write back and both become S; P3's read hits. Final S, I, S with 2 write-backs.

questions.questionText: Under a write-update (write-broadcast) coherence protocol, what happens when a processor writes to a line that other caches also hold?
options: An invalidation is broadcast and every other copy is discarded
The new data is broadcast on the bus and every cache holding the line updates its copy
Only the writer's copy changes; the others keep the old value until the next context switch
The writer stalls until every other cache has evicted the line
questions.explanation: Write-update keeps all copies valid by sending the written word to them. Write-invalidate, as in MESI, instead removes the other copies so that the writer holds the only one.

questions.questionText: For which access pattern does a write-invalidate protocol generate much less bus traffic than a write-update protocol?
options: One processor writes a value once and several processors read it immediately afterwards
One processor writes the same block many times before any other processor reads it
Several processors only read a block that nobody ever writes
Each processor uses only data that no other processor ever caches
questions.explanation: Write-invalidate pays one invalidation and then writes locally, whereas write-update broadcasts every write. For write-once, read-by-many data write-update does better, and in the last two cases neither protocol generates coherence traffic.

questions.questionText: Block Z is held in the Shared state by the caches of P1, P2 and P3. P1 then writes Z six times in a row, after which P2 and P3 each read Z once. Count one bus transaction for each invalidation, each update broadcast and each read miss (a write-back that services a miss is part of that miss). How many bus transactions does a write-invalidate protocol need, compared with a write-update protocol?
questions.explanation: Write-invalidate: one invalidation on the first write, five local hits, then read misses by P2 and P3, giving 3. Write-update: six update broadcasts, after which both reads hit, giving 6.

questions.questionText: Processors P1 and P2 repeatedly update two different variables, a and b, that lie in the same 64-byte cache block. Their MESI caches show heavy invalidation traffic although no data is actually shared. What is the problem, and what is a remedy?
options: True sharing; protect a and b with one common lock
Capacity misses; double the cache size
Deadlock; acquire the locks in a fixed order
False sharing; place a and b in different cache blocks, for example by padding
questions.explanation: Coherence works on whole blocks, so each write to a invalidates P2's copy of the block that also holds b, and vice versa. Separating the variables into different blocks stops the ping-pong.

questions.questionText: In the software coherence scheme that uses a centralised global table set up by the compiler (Mano), each memory block is marked read-only (RO) or read-write (RW). Which rule applies?
options: RO blocks may be copied into all caches, but an RW block may be in only one cache
RW blocks may be copied into all caches, but an RO block may be in only one cache
Both RO and RW blocks may be in every cache, and the table is consulted only on a write
Neither RO nor RW blocks may be cached; the table replaces the caches
questions.explanation: Copies of read-only data can never disagree, so they may be cached everywhere; allowing each writable block in only one cache means it can never have two different cached values.

questions.questionText: A 256-processor NUMA machine connects its nodes through a point-to-point switching network with no shared bus. Which cache coherence approach is appropriate?
options: Write-through caches with no coherence mechanism
questions.explanation: Snooping needs a broadcast medium that every cache can watch. Without a bus, and at this scale, a directory records the sharers of each block and sends invalidations only to them.

questions.questionText: Which statement about snoopy cache coherence is NOT correct?
options: Every cache controller must observe every transaction on the shared bus
It is well suited to a small bus-based symmetric multiprocessor
It scales easily to hundreds of processors because invalidations are sent only to the caches that hold the block
MESI is an example of a snoopy write-invalidate protocol
questions.explanation: Snooping broadcasts every coherence transaction to all caches, so bus bandwidth and snoop load limit it to modest processor counts. Sending invalidations only to the sharers is what a directory does.

questions.questionText: In a 32-processor system with a full-map directory, block B is cached in the Shared state by P4, P9 and P20. P7 now writes B. To how many caches must the directory send invalidation messages?
questions.explanation: The presence bits identify exactly the three sharers, P4, P9 and P20, so three invalidations are sent. A snooping bus would instead broadcast to all 31 other caches.

questions.questionText: A full-map directory keeps one presence bit per processor and one dirty bit for every memory block. For 16 processors and 32-byte blocks, how much storage does the directory add, as a percentage of main-memory capacity?
questions.explanation: Each entry has 16 + 1 = 17 bits for 32 × 8 = 256 data bits, so the overhead is 17/256 = 6.64 %. Forgetting the dirty bit gives 6.25 %, and comparing bits with bytes gives 53.1 %.

questions.questionText: A NUMA machine has 64 processors and 4 GiB of main memory with 128-byte blocks. A full-map directory stores 64 presence bits and 1 dirty bit for every block. How much storage does the directory need (1 MiB = 2^20 bytes)?
questions.explanation: Blocks = 2^32 / 2^7 = 2^25; directory = 65 × 2^25 bits = 65 × 2^22 bytes = 260 MiB, about 6.3 % of memory. Without the dirty bit it would be 256 MiB, and 2,080 is the size in mebibits.

questions.questionText: A 256-processor system compares a full-map directory (one presence bit per processor plus a dirty bit) with a limited-pointer directory that stores up to 4 processor numbers plus a dirty bit for each block. How many bits does each entry need, and how much smaller is the limited-pointer entry?
options: 257 bits versus 1,025 bits, about four times larger
questions.explanation: Full map: 256 + 1 = 257 bits. Limited pointer: 4 × log2 256 + 1 = 4 × 8 + 1 = 33 bits, so the entry is 1 − 33/257 = 87 % smaller.
